subject: query about prediction using computationally cheaper method

messages.author: 7f7355d1143e7e9f
messages.subject: query about prediction using computationally cheaper method
parts:
Hi everyone,

When reading this post (https://punama.github.io/BDI_INLA/), I found a computationally cheaper method for prediction as follows:

#create the spatial structure
sfield_nodes <- model$summary.random$spatial.field['mean']
field <- (Aprediction %*% as.data.frame(sfield_nodes)[, 1])

#make empty matrix to fill predictions
pred <- matrix(NA, nrow = dim(Aprediction)[1], ncol = 1)

## Calculate Predicted values using regression formula
pred <- model$summary.fixed['Intercept', 'mean'] +
  model$summary.fixed['Access', 'mean'] * Access +
  model$summary.fixed['Elevation', 'mean'] * Elevation +
  model$summary.fixed['EVI', 'mean'] * EVI +
  model$summary.fixed['LST_day', 'mean'] * LST_day +
  field

# write results in csv
results <- exp(pred)/(1+exp(pred))

the code uses the mean of the fixed and random coefficience to calculate the mean predictor and then tranforms it to the respose scale using a inverse link function.  I was wondering how to obtain the 95% credible interval and sd of the response-scale prediction. Thanks very much.

steven

messages.author: 66ed4f72a898a51c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] query about prediction using computationally cheaper method
parts:
Hi, 

When you fit the model for the observed data you can ask inla() to return the configurations. Then you can use the inla.posterior.sample() to draw samples and compute what you have computed with the posterior mean of each model term for each sample drawn. Then you can compute credible intervals, or some other functional, with these samples. This is easier if you use the inlabru package as illustrated here: https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/web/random_fields_2d.html

Elias

Thanks for your instant reply, Finn. A further question: I'm not sure about the specific element of "latent" list of my samples ( s1 <- inla.posterior.sample(n=1000,result=output)), for instance, there are five parts for the rowname of the latent: APredictor,  Predictor, st.field, las, gam, rf, and intercept, with the number of 7732, 10708, 22820, 7727, 7727, 7727, and 1, respectively.     control.group = list(model = "ar1")) + f(las, model = "clinear",
    range = c(0, 1), initial = 0.2) + f(gam, model = "clinear",
    range = c(0, 1), initial = 0.2) + f(rf, model = "clinear",
    range = c(0, 1), initial = 0.2)

steven

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] query about prediction using computationally cheaper method
parts:
When using inla.stack, it's really only the APredictor you should
access directly (unless you know the details of the internal model
representation), and the indexing into APredictor is the order that
you specified your predictor;
use inla.stack.index(stack, tag = ...) to find out which indices of
APredictor correspond to a specific sub-stack with a given tag.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] query about prediction using computationally cheaper method
parts:
Hi,
Short answer: we developed the inlabru interface partly to make this easier for spatial model than hand-coding the stack usage, and to make general prediction with posterior samples easier. The generate() and predict() methods, together with the component and bru_mapper systems takes care of the needed mappings.
See the spatial examples on the inlabru GitHub.I’m pages (see link from inlabru.org)

Finn

﻿thanks, Finn. Actually, my  purpose of using  inla.posterior.sample is not to access APredictor (which I know how to). What I would like to do is to predict at new locations. Hence, I need to use one simulation of the fixed (i.e., intercept in my case) and random (i.e., las, gam, and rf in my case) coefficience to calculated linear predictor at the new locations according to my lina.formula ( Y.elect ~ -1 + Intercept + f(st.field, model = local.spde, group = st.field.group,  control.group = list(model = "ar1")) + f(las, model = "clinear", range = c(0, 1), initial = 0.2) + f(gam, model = "clinear",  range = c(0, 1), initial = 0.2) + f(rf, model = "clinear", range = c(0, 1), initial = 0.2)), and then repeat, for instance, 1000 times; that is,

pred.new <- intercept + ['coefficience for las]*las.new +  [' coefficience for gam']*gam.new +  [' coefficience  for rf']*rf.new + field.new

I can get access to the "intecept" and "field.new" via "intecept" and "st.field" lable in the latent of a sample (i.e., s1 <-  inla.posterior.sample(n=1,result=output)), because there is only one "intecept" in latent of a sample, however, I cannot figure out the coefficiences for las, gam, rf as there are 7727 for each (recall i mentioned above: 
"there are several parts for the rowname of the latent: APredictor,  Predictor, st.field, las, gam, rf, and intercept, with the number of 7732, 10708, 22820, 7727, 7727, 7727, and 1, respectively.")

would you please help me out and give some suggestions on predicting using inla.posterior.sample?

steven






On Thursday, February 9, 2023 at 1:00:35 AM UTC+8 Finn Lindgren wrote:
When using inla.stack, it's really only the APredictor you should
access directly (unless you know the details of the internal model
representation), and the indexing into APredictor is the order that
you specified your predictor;
use inla.stack.index(stack, tag = ...) to find out which indices of
APredictor correspond to a specific sub-stack with a given tag.

Finn

One easy way to get access to these is to use the ...eval() function

like

> r=inla(y ~ 1 + x, data=data.frame(y=rnorm(10),x=rnorm(10)),
control.compute=list(config=TRUE))
> xx=inla.posterior.sample(10,r)
> inla.posterior.sample.eval(function() { return (c(x, Predictor)) },
xx)


the 'clinear' model will give the coefficient in the hyperparameters,
here 'Beta for x',


fun[11] 0.37649952060 -0.26018493646
